questions.topic: Normal Forms 1NF-3NF: Removing Redundancy
questions.question: What does the functional dependency X → Y assert about a table?
options: Any two rows that agree on the columns in X must also agree on Y
Any two rows that agree on the columns in Y must also agree on X
The columns in X must be declared as the table's primary key
The columns in Y must each contain a single atomic value per row

questions.topic: Normal Forms 1NF-3NF: Removing Redundancy
questions.question: Which specific defect does Third Normal Form eliminate that Second Normal Form still allows?
options: A non-key column that depends on only part of a composite key
A column that packs several values into one comma-separated string
A non-key column that depends on another non-key column
A key column whose value is duplicated across several tables

questions.topic: Normal Forms 1NF-3NF: Removing Redundancy
questions.question: A table `order_lines(order_id, line_no, customer_id, qty)` has primary key (order_id, line_no), and customer_id is determined by order_id alone. Which normal form does it violate, and why?
options: 1NF, because customer_id is not stored as an atomic single value
2NF, because customer_id depends on a proper subset of the composite key
3NF, because customer_id depends transitively on another non-key column
BCNF, because customer_id functionally determines part of the composite key

questions.topic: Normal Forms 1NF-3NF: Removing Redundancy
questions.question: In a flat order-line table, `product_name` is determined by `product_sku`, and neither column is part of the key. Which decomposition removes this transitive dependency?
options: Move qty and unit_price into a separate table keyed by order_id
Add product_name to the composite primary key of the order-line table
Store product_name as a repeated field inside each order-line row
Split out a products table keyed by product_sku that holds product_name

questions.topic: Normal Forms 1NF-3NF: Removing Redundancy
questions.question: A 3NF schema keeps `unit_price` on each order line even though the products table already stores `list_price`. Why is this duplication considered correct modeling rather than a normalization failure?
options: Numeric columns are exempt from normal-form rules, so copies are permitted
Foreign keys cannot reference price columns, so the value has to be inlined
The captured price describes the sale event itself, not the product entity
The products table is too small for a join against it to be worth running

questions.topic: Normal Forms 1NF-3NF: Removing Redundancy
questions.question: A teammate stores tags as the string `"red,sale,clearance"` in one column, arguing the data is still all there. What capability has actually been lost?
options: The engine can no longer index, join on, or constrain individual tag values
The table can no longer declare any primary key because tags are not unique
The rows can no longer be persisted in a columnar format on disk
The table now contains a transitive dependency between tag and row key

questions.topic: Update Anomalies: What Normalization Prevents
questions.question: What is an update anomaly?
options: A write that fails because a foreign-key constraint rejects the new value
A fact stored in many rows, changed in some of them and missed in others
A row that cannot be inserted until an unrelated parent row exists first
A delete of one fact that silently destroys a different fact sharing its row

questions.topic: Update Anomalies: What Normalization Prevents
questions.question: In a flat order-line table where product facts live only inside order rows, you cannot record a new product until someone orders it. Which anomaly is this?
options: An update anomaly, since product rows would need mass rewriting
A deletion anomaly, since removing the orders would remove the product too
A key anomaly, since the product has no candidate key of its own
An insertion anomaly, since one entity's facts depend on another's rows

questions.topic: Update Anomalies: What Normalization Prevents
questions.question: An email change for a customer requires updating 812 denormalized rows, and the job crashes after 640. What is the resulting state?
options: The table asserts two different emails for one customer, and joins return either
The transaction rolls back automatically, so all 812 rows keep the old email
The engine detects the duplicate fact and rejects further reads of that customer
The remaining 172 rows are locked until the update job is manually restarted

questions.topic: Update Anomalies: What Normalization Prevents
questions.question: Deleting a customer's only order from a flat order table also erases the only record of that customer's email address. What does this demonstrate?
options: A cascade delete that was misconfigured on the foreign-key relationship
An update anomaly caused by editing multiple redundant rows in place
A deletion anomaly, where removing one fact destroys an unrelated fact
An insertion anomaly, where the email could never be stored correctly

questions.topic: Update Anomalies: What Normalization Prevents
questions.question: Why is a read-only analytics copy that is rebuilt nightly from a normalized source immune to update anomalies even though it contains massive redundancy?
options: Because its redundant values are protected by check constraints in the warehouse
Because analytics engines automatically deduplicate repeated values at query time
Because read-only tables physically reject any UPDATE statement issued to them
Because it is never edited in place; every rebuild re-derives each value

questions.topic: Update Anomalies: What Normalization Prevents
questions.question: A chunk store copies each source document's title onto every chunk row. The title is later corrected upstream, and users now see the old title in citations. Which classic defect does this reproduce?
options: A deletion anomaly, because the old title should have been removed first
An update anomaly, because the copied titles go stale until rewritten
An insertion anomaly, because new chunks cannot be added without a title
A join fan-out, because each chunk multiplies the document's title rows

questions.topic: Deliberate Denormalization: Paying Storage to Eliminate Joins
questions.question: What does deliberate denormalization fundamentally relocate?
options: Storage cost, from the fact table to the much smaller dimension tables
Redundancy, from the write path into the query optimizer's join planning
Join computation, from every read to a single step performed at write time
Consistency checks, from application code into database constraints

questions.topic: Deliberate Denormalization: Paying Storage to Eliminate Joins
questions.question: Which two properties of analytical workloads make denormalization a favorable trade there?
options: Reads vastly outnumber writes, and columnar storage compresses repeated values cheaply
Writes vastly outnumber reads, and row storage keeps related values physically adjacent
Queries touch every column, and repeated strings are stored once per table globally
Data never changes after load, and joins are impossible in distributed engines

questions.topic: Deliberate Denormalization: Paying Storage to Eliminate Joins
questions.question: You add a dictionary-encoded `customer_region` column, roughly one byte per row, to a 100-million-row orders table. Approximately how much storage does this cost?
options: Around 10 GB, roughly doubling the size of the orders table
Around 1 GB, comparable to the size of the customers table
Around 1 TB, since every string is stored fully in every row
Around 100 MB, trivial next to re-running the join on every query

questions.topic: Deliberate Denormalization: Paying Storage to Eliminate Joins
questions.question: Months after denormalizing, a team notices region reports disagree with the CRM. They had been hand-editing the wide table whenever customers moved. What was the root mistake?
options: Choosing dictionary encoding, which silently drops updated region values
Treating the derived wide table as the system of record and editing it in place
Failing to add a foreign key from the wide table back to the customers table
Refreshing the wide table too often, overwriting the manual corrections

questions.topic: Deliberate Denormalization: Paying Storage to Eliminate Joins
questions.question: For which system would denormalizing customer attributes onto every order row be the worst fit?
options: A nightly-loaded warehouse serving thousands of dashboard reads per day
A write-heavy operational store where customer attributes change constantly
A read-only reporting mart rebuilt from upstream sources every morning
A batch export feeding a BI tool that cannot execute joins efficiently

questions.topic: Deliberate Denormalization: Paying Storage to Eliminate Joins
questions.question: Chunk rows in a retrieval corpus carry copied document metadata for query-time speed. What keeps this redundancy trustworthy rather than a slow-motion consistency bug?
options: The metadata columns are marked immutable so writers cannot alter them
The retriever re-verifies metadata against the source on every query
Ingestion rebuilds the chunk rows, so drift is bounded by pipeline latency
The copied fields are hashed so any divergence is detected by the database

questions.topic: Nested and Repeated Fields (STRUCT/ARRAY) as Modern Denormalization
questions.question: An `items ARRAY<STRUCT<sku STRING, qty INT64>>` column breaks a classic normalization rule. Which rule, and what keeps the design safe anyway?
options: It breaks 1NF atomicity, but the nested fields are declared in the schema
It breaks 2NF, but the array index acts as the missing part of the composite key
It breaks 3NF, but the struct fields cannot depend on one another transitively
It breaks BCNF, but the engine forbids arrays from determining key columns

questions.topic: Nested and Repeated Fields (STRUCT/ARRAY) as Modern Denormalization
questions.question: What does `UNNEST(items)` do in a query over a table with a repeated field?
options: Merges all arrays in the table into one global list before filtering rows
Converts the array into a comma-separated string for display purposes
Removes duplicate elements from each row's array before aggregation
Expands each row's array into one row per element, restoring child grain

questions.topic: Nested and Repeated Fields (STRUCT/ARRAY) as Modern Denormalization
questions.question: Compared with flattening orders and their lines into one wide table, what duplication does nesting the lines as an array of structs avoid?
options: Repeating each line's sku across every order that ever sold that product
Repeating the array's element type declaration once per row in the schema
Repeating order-level columns like customer and timestamp on every line
Repeating the primary key of the products table inside each struct element

questions.topic: Nested and Repeated Fields (STRUCT/ARRAY) as Modern Denormalization
questions.question: A query aggregates `items.unit_price` across a billion nested order rows. What does the engine physically read?
options: Every order row in full, because nested data is stored as one blob per row
Only that leaf field's column stripe, plus metadata to reassemble rows
The parent columns plus the whole items array, decoded row by row
A materialized flat copy of the table that the engine maintains internally

questions.topic: Nested and Repeated Fields (STRUCT/ARRAY) as Modern Denormalization
questions.question: Line items must now be updated individually many times per day, and support staff query single items across all orders. What should change in the model?
options: Keep the array but add an index on the struct's status field for fast lookups
Keep the array but shrink it by moving static fields into the parent row
Deepen the nesting so each item carries its own array of status events
Promote items to a separate child table, since they are now first-class entities

questions.topic: Nested and Repeated Fields (STRUCT/ARRAY) as Modern Denormalization
questions.question: A pipeline patches one element of a 200-element array in wide nested rows, and write throughput collapses. Why?
options: Mutating one element rewrites the whole parent row, so each patch pays for 200
Array writes acquire a table-level lock, so patches serialize behind every read
The engine re-sorts the whole array on each write to keep elements ordered
Each patch triggers UNNEST, which materializes 200 rows before writing one
